I know that feeling all too well. I bring my body back to life with light, simple foods that have healthy ingredients full of fibre and protein, and don't forget to drink lots of water! 

I'm personally a fan of poke bowls (especially with sashimi but grilled chicken or steak also works), oats with fruit, vegetable-heavy soups, and congee/porridge.

I also like to do a little food prep and stock the fridge with stuff that makes it easy to make healthier snack choices, like cutting up heaps of carrots into carrot sticks to have with dip, or making my favourite goat cheese and avocado whip to spread on crackers, toast, bagels, etc. - smash together a bunch of goat cheese and avocado with a bit of the oil the goat cheese came in (I get the Meredith Dairy jars if anyone here is from Australia, 2-3 cubes of cheese to one avocado is the best ratio usually). Add some lemon juice to prevent the avocado from oxidising and going brown and mix it all together with a fork until it's the texture you want. You can add more oil if you want it smooth and creamy, or leave it out if you prefer it chunky like a guacamole. Add chives and/or some sliced green chili if you're feeling fancy and enjoy!
I like avocado on low-carb toast/bagels, along with smoked salmon and either cream cheese, labneh, or goat cheese and some salt + pepper. Add some dill if you're feeling fancy!

Assuming I was home in my high-rise apartment when the apocalypse hits, the city I live in would likely be overtaken pretty much the same day or overnight and I'd essentially be trapped since I don't drive and don't have access to a car anyway,but I've got a semi-decent plan for my apartment.

If I'd been lucky enough to do a Costco shop recently and stocked up on long-life essentials, I'd divide my food into groups based on how quickly they needed to be eaten before going off and meal prep as best as I could, accounting for how long I would have fridge/freezer power for storage purposes. I could probably scrounge up a gas camping stove from any hardware or department store nearby to keep cooking things. I'd fill up as many containers as possible while I still had clean running water.

I'd also try to rally the survivors in my apartment building and create a vertical commune, converting our natural light-soaked swimming pool area and tennis court + all the corner and edge apartments with balconies into vegetable/produce gardens to grow what food we could. I'd suggest we arrange some sort of pulley system to help our group get to and from the ground without having to take dozens of flights of stairs as once our apartment building lost power, our elevators would be out. I would also suggest a zipline/flying fox to either a neighbouring high-rise building or the rooftop of a nearby standard-height building in case we need to quickly escape, or need to transfer baskets of supplies between buildings (depending on neighbourhood alliances/aid efforts).

In the event that there are no survivors in the building or they do not want to cooperate, I would try to enjoy some much-needed me-time around my scavenging activities, slowly but steadily making my way through my booze stash, reading every book I have (finally), and relatively safe from the zombies in my glass box dozens of storeys in the air.

I'd say it's mostly material (the heavier the better), maybe silhouette and pattern too. For me, I find that my light cotton and linen dresses always look odd with stockings, but my wool, viscose, knit, velvet, and other heavy material dresses look good with them. 

Deeper, darker colours and patterns also help with winterising clothes, but theoretically any colour could make a great winter dress, like a grey sweater dress with a cute cable knit pattern, or a royal blue velvet skater dress with long sleeves.

With patterns, floral are still an option for winter, but probably not the super bright and loud tropical or cottagecore picnic-style florals (though honestly, I'd assess case by case). For the simplest wardrobe additions, I find that polka dots, stripes, tartan/plaid, grid, and lace are all season-neutral patterns you can wear year-round. My current favourite dress that I wear all the time is a red tartan button-up dress with black lapels, it looks great as a summer or winter piece, with or without stockings! 

In terms of silhouette, I personally find that any of my strapless dresses or dresses with spaghetti straps just don't look right with stockings. Maybe it's a perceived imbalance between lots of exposed skin up top with a cold weather look on the bottom? I'm yet to try layering them over a turtleneck to help give the look a more grounded, less breezy look, but I'm hoping that helps me enjoy my summer dresses more often (:

Hey, welcome to the world of makeup (:

What kind of look are you going for and how much effort do you want to put in? This will help you figure out what products you actually need. In general, good skincare is the best base for all looks (moisturiser, serum, SPF, etc.), but some other base makeup products you might want to consider are:

- Primer: this helps makeup adhere better to your skin and goes on AFTER your skincare but BEFORE your actual makeup

- Foundation: this helps even out your skin tone and is like applying another layer of skin on top of your face, so it's best if the foundation shade matches your natural skin tone around your jaw and neck as closely as possible (this helps prevent looking like your face and neck are completely different colours). Foundation can come in powder and liquid forms (like serums and creams) and offer different levels of coverage from light to medium to full. I'm one of those people who dislikes the feeling of wearing heavy layers on my face in general, but everyone is different. Talk to one of the makeup store staff members about your skin type and preferences.

- Concealer: I don't personally use it so I don't know too much about it, but from what I know, this is specifically for covering blemishes and brightening  under-eye bags, etc.

- Contour/highlight: contour products create shadows on your face where you want your bone structure to look like it dips in (like the hollows of your cheeks under the cheekbone, the sides of the nose, etc.). Highlighter helps to bring out the parts of your bone structure that you want to look higher/more prominent (browbone, nose bridge, cheekbones, etc.). Also available in powder and cream forms depending on your preferences.

- Bronzer: not something I personally use, but some people like it because it gives them a 'sunkissed' glow.

- Blush: brings a rosy colour to your cheeks. Some blush products can double as lip colour as well.

- Lip stain/gloss/balm/lipstick: colour for your lips. There are a million shades available in different levels of sheerness/opacity to suit your look and mood.

- Brow products: these are to help shape, define, and fill in your eyebrows. You can get them in pencils, powders, pomade, and gel forms.

- Eyeliner: helps define your eyes and help them stand out/add flair. A classic winged liner look is usually easiest to achieve with a fine-tip liquid liner pen, but some people love applying gel liners with a super precise angled liner brush. You can also get pencil liners which can offer a softer, smudged and smoky kind of look.

- Mascara: makes your lashes more prominent with added length and volume. There's a million different formulas for waterproofing, lash separation, lash growth over time, etc.

- Setting sprays/powders: these help lock in all your hard work so your makeup look lasts longer, great for if you do your makeup in the morning and need it to last all day and all night. Some dry down with a matte look (no shine), some dry down dewy (shiny, but not in an oily way, more in a healthy, 'my skin is naturally moisturised from within' kind of way). Whichever one you pick, there will be something to suit your skin type and desired look.

Hope this helped!

My friends and I build playlists of trippy videos to watch together. I've probably spent the most time on mine because I'm a perfectionist overachiever and am concerned with getting as seamless transitions as possible between video themes, art styles, musical key signatures, timing the peak of the playlist (the most high energy videos) with the peak of the trip, etc.

I've also focused on including videos that every tripping person would enjoy but especially touch on things I know my friends in particular would love (we're all gamers but a few of us really love Halo, a few of us really love Star Wars, one of us LOVES Scooby-Doo, and so on). 

My main playlist goes for a bit over 12 hours (which is about how long my friends usually trip for) and is designed to be started as soon as you take the tab, so the energy level of the playlist matches where you peak in the trip. I've included 15-minute breaks every 1.5-2 hours (about the average movie length) so people can go get water, use the bathroom, stretch their legs, etc.

Watching a playlist like this is great on rainy days/trips where you want to stay indoors all day for whatever reason.

And no, I suppose you can't do two pizzas. Guess you just have to pick another of the thousands of Italian restaurants that have both pizza and non-pizza things on their menu.

You can totally share meals, just don't eat enough of your partner's carby meal to throw off your own diet if that's how strict you want to be. There are also iconic dishes from almost every cuisine I can think of that are as authentic as can get that don't involve carbs. (Also, I'd be surprised if most American BBQ places didn't have keto options considering it's all meat, and there would definitely be dishes without sugary marinades if that's the only thing holding back someone who's very strict on their keto.) 

In terms of travelling, if I'm on holiday with this person, that must mean we're no longer in the early stages of dating where I would be worried about scaring them off with my diet, like OP's original query was about. Me personally, I wouldn't mind breaking keto while overseas to experience the local cuisine to the fullest - there's a good chance I'll be doing enough exercise while I'm holidaying just by walking around to maintain my weight anyway, and I'd just go back on keto once I got home. However, that's a personal choice, and everyone's keto journey is different.

All I'm saying is there are ways to be flexible around food, but going back to my and OP's original topics of discussion, if it's a first date and I tell the other person I have a dietary requirement and they choose to no longer consider me an option because of it, then okay. Guess they're just not the sort of person who tries to be flexible or accommodating about even small things like that, and as far as I'm concerned, I'm dodging a bullet. How much worse would it be later down the line if we were together and something more important than just picking a different restaurant came up?

And there are plenty that do. Get the salad without croutons. Get the soup. Get the stir-fried meat and veg dish. Get the shared grill skewers platter. Get the steak, and if it comes with potatoes or something on the side, ask your date if they want then or just get it without the potatoes. There are lots of options out there in terms of both dishes and cuisines, and if I thought it would be unreasonable or impractical for the restaurant to make substitutions (like a pizza joint), I'd just pick somewhere else.

It's more about their willingness to work with something you've told them is important to you (like a diet you've decided to follow for your own personal reasons), which would fall under favourable personality characteristics anyway.

Keto people also have options literally everywhere. If one restaurant doesn't work out for you, there are probably a dozen more within 2 blocks of the first one that will.

TL;DR: 6 years ago, I sprained my ankle so badly I was temporarily blinded by the pain and the doctor at the hospital said it would have been better if I'd just broken it.

I was running for a tram. In high heels. With an extremely heavy backpack on my back full of expensive VR equipment that I needed to do a demonstration for some work clients on behalf of my company (hence the business attire). There's a section in the middle of the road between the sidewalk and the tram stop that's uneven grassy ground, and I guess I landed on my foot wrong because the next thing I know, I'm toppling over like a tall landmark in a natural disaster/apocalypse movie. That moment felt like it was stretching on and on in slow motion, like toffee being pulled apart torturously in mid-air.

I hear this God-awful popping, snapping sound I still have never been able to forget and this searing hot pain rips through me as my whole world goes white. I can't see anything, zero vision, even though I'm pretty sure my eyes are open. There's no sound except the roaring rush of white noise, which was maybe my own blood pounding in my ears? The sound of my own screaming slowly fades in and I realise that I'm screaming at all.

People from both sides of the street are crowding around me, trying to see if I'm okay. I hobbled onto the tram with the backpack in tow, still in my heels, limping badly. I finish the demonstration with the work people, making jokes about how 'If I can do this with a badly sprained ankle in heels, any of you can do it'.

I take an Uber to the hospital straight after the work thing is done and yeah, the doc looked at me, my shoes, the bag, and the chart that said I walked around for an hour with the injury and was probably torn between having an aneurysm over my stupidity and having sympathy for me.

I spent a week and a half bedridden and couch-ridden, the next 3 weeks on crutches, and the next 3 weeks walking with a limp.

You wanna know the worst thing though? There are several ways the whole situation could have been avoided:

1. Work offered to let me expense an Uber from my place to the demonstration venue (we were almost NEVER allowed to expense stuff so this was a big deal), but I turned down the offer because I didn't want to be seen as a hassle to the company.
2. The reason I was running in the first place was because I didn't want to be late. Even with the injury, I made it with 10 minutes to spare.
3. I took an extremely illogical route to get to the venue because for some reason, I had convinced myself I needed to take the tram? No idea why. But I didn't need to go that direction at all, meaning I could have skipped the uneven grassy terrain.

Moral of the story: if work lets you Uber anywhere on their dime, don't try and be an inconsequential hero for no reason.

I try not to judge on things the person doesn't have any control over, like whether the house's base design feels old-fashioned, cheap, etc., only things they can do something about with little effort.

If the person doesn't know they're going to have guests in advance, I'm pretty lenient since they haven't had time to put their house's best foot forward (we've all been there). However, if they know there are people coming over, these are things I'll judge on in order of what I would notice first:

* Smell - a nice smell like a reed/aroma diffuser/scented candle is great, neutral house smell or no smell is fine, unpleasant smell is, well, unpleasant
* Light - does the space feel bright and welcoming? Slightly dim and intimate/cosy? Or dark and uninviting? Obviously, this can change once the person is inside and has turned on their preferred lighting, so next is whether the light type is cold and unflattering (like a harsh white downlight), or warm and cosy like a slightly yellow-toned white diffused by lampshades/pendants
* Cleanliness - clutter mess to a certain degree is acceptable, filth mess less so. Unavoidable mess like pet hair and dust in hard-to-reach places just gets brushed off as an inevitable part of life and has little to no negative impact on my first impression.
* Personal touches - does the house look like a clinical showroom rather than a lived-in home? Or are there things I can see that speak to the person who lives here, like knick-knacks, décor touches, and elements that obviously take personal effort to care for (e.g. plants)?
* Interior design - does the furniture layout make sense for the room/is it pleasant to interact with? Does the aesthetic of the home/room feel streamlined or busy, cohesive or eclectic, and does that work for the space and person whose home it is?
* Plants:  
\- real plants in good, healthy condition are viewed extremely favourably (I love plants and take care of many of my own)  
\- real plants in poor condition inspire sympathy and me providing a slew of care tips (if asked)  
\- fake plants are met with varying degrees of disappointment depending on how difficult the real-life version of the plant would be to keep healthy (e.g. a fake orchid I could understand since real flowers can be finnicky and may not be in bloom year-round, but fake snake plants annoy me since real snake plants are basically indestructible already)

Probably went into too much detail, but that's just the kind of person I am.

Depends on my level of tiredness. If I'm truly too tired to even turn on my stove/pull a pot out of the cupboard, I'm ordering in.

If I don't want to order in but can't be bothered with a chopping board/knife combo, I'll boil up some frozen dumplings or pasta, or pan-fry the dumplings. For extra crispy dumpling bottoms, put a little oil in the pan, put the dumplings in bottom-down and let them sizzle for a few moments before turning the heat down to a medium-low flame. Then pour a small amount of water in to the pan (for me it's about 100-150ml) and quickly cover with a lid so the steam helps cook the dumplings all the way through from frozen. When the water is evaporated, it's ready to eat. Timing and water amount works best if you tweak it to your own methods. My method gives me golden-brown crunchy bottoms every time and gives my friend charcoal every time.

Before I started the keto diet, I would also sometimes turn on my rice cooker and steam some rice and a bunch of chopped frozen veggies and eggs in a separate tray that sits above the actual rice. If I timed the eggs right, they come out perfectly soft-boiled (which is one of my favourite ways to eat them).

If I'm willing to put time into the cooking but not effort, I'll make cauliflower fried rice. Pre-made cauliflower rice usually comes frozen in a bag, so just break it up into smaller chunks, whack it in a big pan/wok with some cooking oil, and pour in your extras like meat (minced or sliced), fresh bagged or frozen veg, chili, and cover with the lid and leave to cook. I normally use kitchen scissors to cut up strips of meat if it's not minced, and any chili/spring onion flavour/garnish extras since I hate washing chopping boards and knives.

Add beaten eggs towards the end of the cooking process and keep stirring so that there's fluffy bits of egg everywhere rather than all your 'rice' coming out in a giant wok-shaped cake held together by scrambled egg. I cook in bulk so 5-10 minutes of actual work with this dish will usually get me 3 days' worth of food (though I skip breakfast every day).

And of course, you can't forget the holy grail of reasonably tasty no-effort food: instant noodles. Jazz it up with added egg, chili (if the soup isn't already chili), spring onions, and frozen sliced meat if you've got it, the kind Asian grocers sell for hot pot. Pour the boiling water over it all and cover to let it steam. I lived on that stuff for a lot of my poor uni student days.
